0135.event: Through the Caucasus gate in Georgia, about three hundred thousand years ago, new waves of humans are moving: the second crossing. The first ones had passed this way long before, and now the latecomers follow, family by family, hunter by hunter, trailing the herds between Africa and Asia. The gate was never truly empty. It stayed a passage, a way through, worn deeper with every passing. The mountains stand behind them, the promise ahead. Dawn on dawn, the road the first had trod grows wider. The second crossing is not as famous as the first, but roads are made by the many who follow, not the few who lead.
0135.announce: Waves through the gate, in a marching verse: The Second Crossing.
0135.title: The Second Crossing
0135.piece:
New waves through the Caucasus gate.
The second crossing. Do not wait.
Follow where the first had gone,
between the dusk and the dawn.
The herds move, and we move too,
through the pass the old ones knew.
Three hundred thousand years, the way
grows wider, day by day.
Families, hunters, on the road,
each one carrying their load.
The gate was never truly still.
It hums with feet upon the hill.
The first found it. The rest made wide
the road. Walk on, with pride.

0136.event: In China, about three hundred thousand years ago, the descendants of Peking Man still keep their hearths against the northern cold. The winters come and go, the ice descends, the hunger circles, but the hearths hold. It is the same flame the ancestors kept, in the same caves, the same defiance of the cold, the same brave refusal to go out. Continuity is the quietest kind of heroism. Nobody sings of the ten thousandth winter survived, but somebody survived it, and then the next. The Zhoukoudian winters were beaten by an unbroken line of tenders, and the fire never slept.
0136.announce: The flame held on, in a winter song: The Zhoukoudian Winters.
0136.title: The Zhoukoudian Winters
0136.piece:
The winters came, the winters went.
The ice, the hunger, the descent
of snow. But the hearths held true.
The flame kept me. It kept you.
Peking Man's children, brave and bold,
still keep the fire against the cold.
Three hundred thousand years, the same
cave, the same unbroken flame.
The tenders never let it sleep.
The watch they kept was long and deep.
Continuity, the quiet art:
to keep the fire is to keep the heart.
The winters lost. The hearths won.
We keep the flame. We carry on.

0137.event: On Java's Solo River, about three hundred thousand years ago, the last of the Asian erectus gather by the water. A million years on Java, and now the end, not with a bang but with the slow fading of a kind. They were people: they lived, they loved, they knew the river, the humid weather, the morning songs of the forest. Stand among the last in the mind's eye, and the weight of the long past is there. Bow to them. The Solo River still moves, the sun still yellows the water, but the fires of the last ones have gone out one by one. A whole way of being human, closed like a book.
0137.announce: A farewell verse for the last of Java: The Solo River People.
0137.title: The Solo River People
0137.piece:
On the Solo River, the last ones stand,
the Asian erectus, of the old land.
A million years on Java's shore,
and now, the end. They are no more.
Not with a bang, but with the slow
fading, the way all endings go.
They lived. They loved. They knew the river.
The humid air, the sweet giver
of life. Three hundred thousand years.
The last ones' hopes, the last ones' fears,
all gone. The water moves along.
The sun still sings its yellow song.
We bow to those who came before.
The Solo keeps them evermore.

0138.event: At Lake Eyasi in Tanzania, about three hundred thousand years ago, new fossils show many human kinds still sharing East Africa. Not one road but many: different bodies, different minds, all reaching, all human. The earth was trying everything at once, and the lake was wide enough for all of it. Walk among the Eyasi kin in the mind's eye, and the diversity is startling. There is room for the cautious and the bold, the tall and the small. We tend to tell the story as a single line, but it was a thicket, a crowd, a hundred experiments at once. The lake watched them all, and kept them.
0138.announce: Many kinds, one lake, a verse: The Eyasi Kin.
0138.title: The Eyasi Kin
0138.piece:
Many kinds around one lake.
Not one road, but roads to make.
Three hundred thousand years ago,
the Eyasi waters, wide and slow,
held every kind the earth could try.
The tall, the small, the bold, the shy.
All human. All reaching. All true.
The lake was wide enough for you,
for me, for all the kinds that came.
No single road. No single name.
The earth was trying everything.
The lake heard every song they'd sing.
A thicket, not a line, we grew.
The many made the one that's you.

0139.event: In the Omo Valley of Ethiopia, about three hundred thousand years ago, the fossils edge closer to the modern form. The old world's ledge is giving way. Walk the valley floor in the mind's eye, and the future knocks at the door: the forerunners, not quite us, but near, so near you could almost hear them speak. Not yet, but soon. The modern shape emerges bone by bone, and the valley holds the proof that we came from somewhere. We came from here, from these, year on year. The forerunners ran ahead, and we followed, and the following has never stopped.
0139.announce: Almost us, in a valley verse: The Omo Forerunners.
0139.title: The Omo Forerunners
0139.piece:
In the Omo Valley, the bones draw near
to us. The future's almost here.
Three hundred thousand years ago,
the forerunners began to show
the modern shape, bone by bone.
The old world's ledge was overthrown.
Not quite us, but near, so near.
You can almost hear them, dear
reader, speaking. Not yet. But soon.
They walked beneath the same moon.
The valley holds where we began.
The forerunners. Almost man.
We followed where they led the way.
We follow still, today.

0140.event: By an ancient spring in South Africa, about three hundred thousand years ago, a skull lies in the earth that shows the southern branch of humanity taking modern shape. Kneel beside the Florisbad water in the mind's eye, and the slow shaping is there: the water, the life it brings, the modern form emerging in the south, no fuss, just time and the spring. Drink from that water in the imagination, and it tastes of the future: clear, cold, and true. The spring flows still, for the southern line, for all of us. The water is ancient. The becoming was slow. The result is us.
0140.announce: Water from the deep past, in a song: The Florisbad Spring.
0140.title: The Florisbad Spring
0140.piece:
By the ancient spring, the skull lies deep,
where the southern waters seep.
Three hundred thousand years ago,
the modern shape began to grow.
The Florisbad water, clear and cold,
holds the story, never old.
Kneel beside it. Drink it in.
The future's where we begin.
The southern branch, becoming true,
the water shaped both me and you.
No fuss, no rush, just time and spring.
The water taught the everything
we are. It flows. It always will.
The ancient spring is flowing still.

0141.event: In the Levant, about three hundred thousand years ago, embers are carried from hearth to hearth, wrapped and guarded on the journey. No band need ever be without flame now, from birth to death. Walk beside the carrier in the mind's eye: the ember glowing in moss, the careful hands, the steady pace. It is the oldest portable technology, and the most precious. The fear of the dark, answered by the carried coal. The flame is not yours or mine. It belongs to all, and the carrying is the sharing. Pass it on. That was the whole of the law, and it still is.
0141.announce: Carry the coal, in a keeper's letter: The Fire Carriers.
0141.title: The Fire Carriers
0141.piece:
My fellow keeper, take this coal.
It is wrapped in moss, still alive, still whole.
Carry it well. Walk steady. Do not run.
The flame you bear outshines the sun
to those who wait in the dark ahead.
No band need ever be without, I said,
and I say again: the fire is ours,
not yours, not mine. It has the powers
of life itself. Three hundred thousand years
we have carried it, through hopes and fears.
Pass it on. The art is heart to heart.
Carry the coal. Do your part.

0142.event: In East Africa, about three hundred thousand years ago, the family of humankind stands at a fork. Three ways open: Neanderthals to the north, Denisovans to the east, and our own line rising in Africa. Sisters, brothers, kin, all human, all about to begin the long divergence. Stand at the parting in the mind's eye, and the sorrow is real: goodbye, for now. But the blood would meet again, in bone and gene, in the ancient flood of mixing. For now, three roads. The north, the east, the African sky. Every family has its partings. Ours was the whole world, dividing.
0142.announce: Three roads, one family, a poem: The Great Parting.
0142.title: The Great Parting
0142.piece:
Three roads opened, long ago.
Three ways the human winds would blow.
North, the Neanderthals would go.
East, the Denisovans' cold snow.
And we, from Africa, would rise.
Three hundred thousand years, the skies
watched the parting. Sisters, kin,
all human, all about to begin
apart. Goodbye is hard to say
when the road leads threefold away.
But blood would meet again, in time.
The genes would cross, the bells would chime
of reunion. For now, three ways.
We walk them still, these parted days.

0143.event: At Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about three hundred thousand years ago, some of the earliest faces we have found of our own species look out over the desert. The threshold. Stand beside them in the mind's eye, and you see what they cannot: the everything-to-be, the cities and songs and ships and stars, the healing and the hurting. They look out, and they do not know. But the desert wind still sings, and the faces still look. The story of Homo sapiens begins here, with nothing but the future in their eyes. Cross the threshold with them. We have been crossing it ever since.
0143.announce: Step over, in a threshold song: The Threshold.
0143.title: The Threshold
0143.piece:
At Jebel Irhoud, the faces turn
toward the desert. Watch and learn:
three hundred thousand years ago,
some of the first of us began to know
the world. The threshold. Step across.
No gain without the loss.
They looked out, and they couldn't see
the cities, songs, the you, the me.
But we can see. We stand beside
the first ones, at the desert's wide
expanse. The wind still sings their song.
We've been crossing, all along.
Step over. The story starts.
We carry it in our hearts.

0144.event: In a South African spring deposit, about two hundred ninety-five thousand years ago, a broad-faced fossil skull lies half ancestral and half ours. The brow is heavy, but the braincase is already ours, and the combination is the first hint that we were on our way. Someone knelt here when the water ran clear and died before the story found its words, but the story had already begun in the bone. Lift it in the mind's eye: half a stranger, half a mirror. A face becoming human, forgetting itself into the mud, and remembering itself in us.
0144.announce: Half a stranger, half a mirror, a verse: The Florisbad Skull.
0144.title: The Florisbad Skull
0144.piece:
Broad-faced, from the spring-bed mud,
half stranger, half our blood.
The brow is heavy, deep and old.
The braincase ours, a shape to hold
the future. Two hundred ninety-five
thousand years. It is alive
in us. Someone knelt and died
when the spring ran clear and wide.
The story had begun in bone
before the words were ever known.
A face becoming human, true,
forgetting self, remembering you.
Half mirror. Half stranger. Whole.
The skull still speaks. It holds the soul
of becoming. We are its kin.
The becoming wears us, deep within.

0145.event: At Olorgesailie in Kenya, about two hundred ninety thousand years ago, toolmakers returned to the same lakeshore for a hundred thousand years. Not a settlement, but a place held in memory: the first home before homes. The same fires lit on the same sand by hands a thousand lifetimes apart. A grandmother taught a daughter the good chipping stones, and the daughter taught hers, and the lake kept rising and falling. The footprints layered like pages in a book no one wrote down. They came back because the place was good. We have been coming back to good places ever since.
0145.announce: A hundred thousand years of returning, in verse: The Long Lakeshore.
0145.title: The Long Lakeshore
0145.piece:
The same shore, the same sand,
the same lake, the same land.
A hundred thousand years of feet,
a hundred thousand years of heat
and rain. The toolmakers came back,
year on year, on the same track.
Grandmother taught the daughter true.
The daughter taught her daughter too.
The lake rose. The lake fell.
The place was good. The makers tell,
without a word, the oldest lore:
come back to the good shore.
Not a house, but held in mind.
The first home of humankind.
We return. We always will.
The lakeshore calls us still.

0146.event: At Gademotta in Ethiopia, about two hundred eighty thousand years ago, hunters hauled volcanic obsidian for miles to knap fine blades. The black glass traveled from the volcano's mouth to the hunting ground on strong backs, wrapped in hide: the world's first supply chain, built on tired feet and sharp stone. At the camp, the knappers sat in rows, striking long blades from the midnight stone, while the children gathered the sharpest chips to play. No one told them to trade. No one told them to plan. But the glass was here, and the game was there, and a man with a blade ate better. So they walked.
0146.announce: Black glass on strong backs, a song: The Obsidian Caravans.
0146.title: The Obsidian Caravans
0146.piece:
Black glass from the volcano's mouth,
carried north, carried south.
Two hundred eighty thousand years,
the obsidian caravan appears.
Wrapped in hide, on strong backs borne,
from the dark of night to morn.
At Gademotta, the knappers sit,
striking blades from the black of it.
The flakes fall like dark confetti.
The children grab the sharpest. Ready,
the hunters go. The glass is keen.
The sharpest stone they've ever seen.
No one told them. They just knew:
a man with a blade eats better. True.
The first supply chain, built on feet.
The obsidian made the hunt complete.

0147.event: At Twin Rivers in Zambia, about two hundred sixty-six thousand years ago, someone ground red ochre into powder and rubbed it on the skin. No wall to paint, no cave, just arms and faces and breasts colored with the earth itself, tens of thousands of years before the first cave painting. The dust ran red as blood and stained the fingers that held it. Long before we painted walls, we were already the painted animal. Color worn on the body, for beauty or meaning or both. The red stone says we were decorating ourselves before we had anywhere to hang the art.
0147.announce: Red as blood, in a color verse: The Red Stone.
0147.title: The Red Stone
0147.piece:
Grind the ochre. Make it red.
Rub it on the arms, the head.
Two hundred sixty-six thousand years,
before the cave art, before the fears
of the blank wall. Just skin.
Let the color sink in.
Red as blood, the dust runs true.
The earth has painted me and you.
No wall to paint. No cave to keep.
The color runs both wide and deep.
We were the painted animal first.
The red stone quenched our thirst
for beauty. Wear it. Let it show.
The oldest color. Let it glow.

0148.event: Above the Florisbad spring in South Africa, about two hundred sixty thousand years ago, a broad brow waits in the earth, watching the dry months come and go. The hunters crouched in the muddy shallows and drank where the water ran cold. The rains failed and returned, the herds drifted in and away, and the watcher stayed: a heavy face sunk in the spring-bed, keeping a long and patient vigil. A sentinel no one appointed, guarding a well no one owned, while we were still learning what it meant to be a people at all. The spring gave water. The watcher gave witness.
0148.announce: A sentinel's verse for the patient brow: The Watcher at the Spring.
0148.title: The Watcher at the Spring
0148.piece:
Above the spring, the broad brow waits,
through the dry months, through the fates
of rain. Two hundred sixty thousand years,
the watcher calms the hunters' fears
with water. Crouch and drink it cold.
The story is both new and old.
The rains fail. The rains return.
The herds drift. The fires burn.
The watcher stays, sunk in the bed,
keeping vigil for the dead
and living. No one set the guard.
The spring runs clear. The watch is hard.
A sentinel of mud and bone.
We were not, are not, alone.

0149.event: Deep in the Kabwe mine in Zambia, about two hundred fifty thousand years ago, a heavy-browed skull marks a cousin branch of humanity that did not survive. Big-boned, strong-jawed, built to endure, walking a road that led somewhere else. Not our grandfather, but our uncle's brother: a branch that flowered and fell. The tree of humankind was never a straight trunk. It was a thicket, a tangle, a crowd, and we are only the ones still standing. Hold that skull in the mind's eye, and think of all the cousins whose fires went out. We carry them in the thicket's shade.
0149.announce: A thicket, not a line, a poem: The Cousin at Broken Hill.
0149.title: The Cousin at Broken Hill
0149.piece:
Deep in the mine, the skull is found,
heavy-browed, from the ancient ground.
Two hundred fifty thousand years.
A cousin's face, through hopes and fears.
Not our grandfather. Something more:
the uncle's brother, at the door
of a road that led another way.
He flowered once. He could not stay.
The tree was never straight and tall.
It was a thicket. Crowds would call
it home. We are the standing few.
The fallen shade still covers you.
Hold the skull. Remember well:
not every branch the tale will tell.
But every branch was human, true.
The thicket grew. It grew to you.

0150.event: Across a green Sahara, about two hundred forty thousand years ago, Aterian hunters hafted tanged stone points onto wooden shafts. Rain fell where the desert would one day be, and the hunters shaped stone teeth with stems and bound them to wood: the first true spears, and the hunt changed forever. Watch one take a barbary sheep at twenty paces in the mind's eye, and the whole camp eats. The green Sahara gave, and the hunters took with new reach. The desert came later. The spears came first, and with them, the long arm of the hunt.
0150.announce: Green Sahara, sharp points, a hunting song: The Aterian Hunters.
0150.title: The Aterian Hunters
0150.piece:
Green Sahara, where the rain once fell,
the Aterian hunters knew it well.
Tanged points on wooden shafts,
the first true spears, the new crafts.
Two hundred forty thousand years.
The hunt grew long. The camp still cheers
the hunter home. At twenty paces,
the sheep falls. The hunger erases.
The desert wasn't desert then.
The green was home to hunting men.
They bound the stone teeth to the wood.
The spears flew farther than they could
have dreamed. The hunt was changed that day.
We hunt the Aterian way.

0151.event: Along the Omo River in Ethiopia, about two hundred thirty-three thousand years ago, a volcano spoke, and the ash fell soft as snow. In it waited two skulls: ours, unmistakably ours, the high forehead, the small teeth, the braincase that would one day hold a symphony. Brush the ash away in the mind's eye, and there is the strange vertigo of meeting yourself early. They drank from this river. They watched these birds. They had no name for what they were becoming, but they were becoming us. The ash kept them like a promise. Already, unmistakably, us.
0151.announce: Ash-soft, in a vertigo verse: The Omo Skulls.
0151.title: The Omo Skulls
0151.piece:
The volcano spoke. The ash fell soft.
Two skulls in the river's loft
of time. Two hundred thirty-three
thousand years. Come and see:
ours, unmistakably ours, the brow
high, the teeth small. And now,
the vertigo of meeting you
two hundred millennia too
early. They drank here. They watched the birds.
They had no name, and needed no words.
The ash kept them, a promise sealed.
Already us. Already revealed.
The river runs. The skulls remain.
We are. We were. We are again.

0152.event: Somewhere in Africa, about one hundred fifty thousand years ago, a woman lived whose maternal line reaches every human alive today. The place is lost, the name is lost. She walked, gathered, laughed, bore children, and never knew she carried the future. Her daughters had daughters who had daughters, an unbroken line of mothers, mother to mother, through the ice ages, through famine and flood and fire, until it reaches you. Stand in a hundred ancient camps in the mind's eye and wonder which fire was hers, which laugh, which lullaby. She is the root of us all, and she never knew.
0152.announce: Every mother, in a lineage song: The Mother of All.
0152.title: The Mother of All
0152.piece:
Somewhere in Africa, long ago,
a woman walked where the wild winds blow.
One hundred fifty thousand years.
She laughed. She cried. She knew no fears
of the future, for she couldn't see
the line that runs from her to me,
to you, to every human alive.
Her daughters' daughters still survive
in us. Mother to mother, hand to hand,
the unbroken line across the land.
She never knew. How could she know?
She was the root. She made us grow.
Every mother, every birth,
the grandmother of all the earth.

0153.event: In a seaside cave in Greece, about two hundred ten thousand years ago, a battered human skull lies half-buried in the rock, face to the sea. It may be ours, far earlier than the books once allowed: in Europe a hundred thousand years too soon. Crouch in that cave mouth in the mind's eye, and look out at the same blue water. Our story kept leaking past every border the scholars drew. We were wanderers before we were anything else. We walked farther and earlier than anyone guessed, and the cave kept our secret until the sea air gave it up. The wanderers were always ahead of the map.
0153.announce: Too soon, too far, a verse: The Skull in the Greek Cave.
0153.title: The Skull in the Greek Cave
0153.piece:
Half-buried in the rock, face to the sea,
a battered skull, perhaps as old as we.
Two hundred ten thousand years, too soon,
beneath the Greek sun and moon.
The books said: not yet. The cave said: yes.
We wandered more, and settled less,
than anyone had guessed. The blue
water watched, and the skull knew too:
we were wanderers before the name,
before the border, before the fame.
The secret kept till the sea air
gave it up. We were always there,
ahead of the map, beyond the line.
The wanderers' tale is yours and mine.

0154.event: At Misliya Cave on the Carmel coast, about one hundred ninety-five thousand years ago, a human upper jaw lies in the earth: among the earliest Homo sapiens found outside Africa. Someone chewed and laughed and spoke here, a day's walk from the sea. The great leaving had already begun, foot by foot, generation by generation, long before anyone thought. Touch those teeth in the mind's eye, and the lesson is simple. Every journey starts with somebody just walking a little farther than yesterday. The jaw is the proof. The leaving was already underway, and it never stopped.
0154.announce: A little farther than yesterday, a verse: The Misliya Jaw.
0154.title: The Misliya Jaw
0154.piece:
An upper jaw, human teeth,
in Misliya Cave, where the sea breathes.
One hundred ninety-five thousand years.
Among the first outside. No fears,
just walking, foot by foot, each day
a little farther on the way.
Someone chewed here. Someone laughed.
The great leaving, fore and aft,
had just begun. The sea was near.
The future was already here.
Touch the teeth. The lesson's true:
every journey starts with you
walking just a little more
than yesterday. Open the door.
The leaving never really ends.
We walk. The road extends.
